https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/trave.title: Travel’s 50 biggest winners and losers in 2024
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/trave.subtitle: Notre Dame and the Northern Lights are crowned ‘winners’, while it was a year to forget for Euston and sunbathers in Majorca
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/trave.text:
This year, The Telegraph’s travel experts have explored every corner of the world – from Antarctica to Zambia via Madagascar and Fiji.
It’s been an eventful year. Geopolitical events have redrawn flight routes from east to west, while natural phenomena – from turbulence to heatwaves,  floods to earthquakes – have affected our travels in myriad ways. Some destinations have launched fresh bids to lure new tourists, while others are urging us to stay away.
Here are the 50 winners and losers of 2024, featuring a long-awaited museum in Egypt, a (very) big cruise ship and a log-jammed British national park. Did we miss a winner or loser? Please comment at the bottom of the article to join the conversation.
Finally. After two decades in the making, and 11 years behind schedule, Cairo’s Grand Egyptian Museum opened its doors. With a floor space of 490,000 square metres, this is the world’s largest archaeological museum. Once fully operational, it will be able to hold more than 100,000 items, including the complete collection of artefacts discovered in Tutankhamun’s tomb.
The Dubai-based carrier came out top in our comprehensive ranking and rating of the world’s best airlines. It scored big points for its generous baggage allowance, punctuality record, fleet of roomy double-decker Airbus A380s, and the finest wine list of any airline – plus showers for first-class passengers.
Five years after suffering a devastating fire, Paris’s great medieveal cathedral reopened to the public following an international restoration effort. After the blaze, an estimated €846 million (£701 million) in donations poured in from 150 countries in a surge of solidarity, the “biggest such philanthropic effort in history”, according to Alexandre Giuglaris, head of the French Heritage Foundation.
This long-favoured oasis for New York’s chic set had its moment in the spotlight this year as the setting of the hit Netflix show The Perfect Couple, starring Nicole Kidman, Liev Schreiber and Dakota Fanning. Spare a thought for Chatham, 30 miles up the coast on the Cape Cod Peninsula, where much of the series was actually filmed, but which received none of the credit.
The Norwegian cruise operator won top spot in Friends of the Earth’s “Cruise Ship Report Card”, which rated lines on their environmental credentials. The company scored well for its advanced sewage treatment systems, hybrid ships and efforts in air pollution reduction.
After a noisy public backlash, Manston Airport, once Kent International, was this year  given the green light to reopen after years of closure. Other regional airports, including Southend, Doncaster-Sheffield and Cardiff, are seeing investment that could put them firmly back on the map for British holidaymakers
It has been a vintage year for tourist taxes. Bali introduced a $10 (£8) levy in February, Venice started charging tourists €5 merely to enter the city in April, while here in the UK, Bournemouth became the latest city to charge a room rate – £2 per room, per night – following in the footsteps of Manchester. Amsterdam became the steepest of them all, taxing 12.5 per cent of the room rate per night.
Denmark’s second city was named the world’s happiest by the Institute for Quality of Life. Its Happy City Index acknowledged that “the concept of a ‘happy city’ will always vary depending on individual perspectives”, but after crunching criteria such as education, mobility and access to green spaces, Aarhus came out top.
Once common across Europe, sleeper trains fell into the shadow of planes as the era of budget airlines kicked off in the 1990s. But it’s all change on the railways. Now, a number of fresh routes have emerged, with Austrian operator ÖBB reinstating sleepers from Vienna to cities including Amsterdam, Berlin and Zurich; France restoring trains from Paris to Nice; and Italy investing in a new network.
The grande dame of Bangkok took top spot in our inaugural hotel awards. Lee Cobaj, our destination expert, wrote: “This hotel is loved for its grandeur, exceptional restaurants (from dim sum to Michelin-starred French cuisine) and superb staff, many of whom have worked here for decades.”
The King has expressed his desire to make royal residences more accessible to the public, and he put that into action in 2024. For the first time, visitors can explore the East Wing of Buckingham Palace, including the Centre Room, which leads onto the famous balcony (although tourists cannot actually go onto the balcony itself). Balmoral, in the Scottish Highlands, also opened to the public for the first time, offering access to the previously out-of-bounds interior of the vast castle.
After a somewhat drizzly opening ceremony, the Paris Olympics was regarded as a huge success on a scale similar to Sydney in 2000 and London in 2012. The Telegraph’s Simon Briggs wrote: “The venues have been electric, with every seat filled, every fan invested and every nerve jangled.”
This winter, the Northern Lights are at their “solar maximum”, creating prime conditions for spotting the phenomenon. The aurora was even seen as far south as Brighton during a particularly fierce solar storm that took place in October. More could follow in early 2025.
The affable travel presenter released his brand new BBC travelogue, Wilderness, which received positive reviews across the board. “It’s old-fashioned adventure television, and it’s a privilege to go along for the ride,” wrote The Telegraph’s Benji Wilson.
All eyes have been on Portugal’s exclusive peninsula (nicknamed the “Hamptons of Portugal” or the “Malibu of Europe”) after Prince Harry and Meghan reportedly began eyeing up properties in the area. They would join George Clooney, Sharon Stone and Jose Mourinho, who also have residences on the sunny stretch of coast, just south of Lisbon.
Love it or hate it, the extraordinary Icon of the Seas certainly made a splash. Nicknamed the “human lasagne” after a rendering showcasing its extraordinary scale did the rounds on the internet, the Royal Caribbean vessel set sail in January. With a capacity of 7,600 passengers and a length of 1,197ft (365m), it would be taller than the Shard were you to hoist it upright. The Star of the Seas, due to launch next year, will be a smidgen bigger.
London’s first Underground line emerged as the winner in our survey of the best and worst tube lines in the capital. With air-con, forward-facing seats, good cleanliness and fast-running trains, it pipped the District line (second) and the Jubilee line (third) to the post.
Greenland’s capital city, Nuuk, has a brand new international airport. The new hub means larger aircraft can land on the island for the first time, paving the way for non-stop flights from Europe and the United States. Next year, the northern town of Ilulissat will receive an airport upgrade that will also improve connections.
Women’s retreats are en vogue. One, Camp Château in south-west France, has racked up a 13,000-strong waiting list. Astrology, horse-riding, yoga, bingo, petanque and blindfolded wine-tasting featured during our writer’s visit.
It was a momentous year for Everest anoraks after the National Geographic explorer Jimmy Chin discovered what is believed to be the boot of Andrew “Sandy” Irvine. If it is found to belong to Irvine, it could rewrite the history of mountaineering.
It has been a positive year for the slopes of Norway. There has been a suite of new packages from tour operators, including Crystal Ski and Inghams, plus nine new flight routes to Norway have been launched this winter to meet growing demand, by Tui, British Airways, easyJet and Norwegian, from airports across the UK.
The Asian megahub came out in top spot in our study, ranking and rating the best airports in the world. John Arlidge, the co-author of the article, wrote: “Changi ticks just about every box, from on-time performance (81.6 per cent) to the latest tech. It’s bright and airy, with outdoor terraces, greenery (look out for the butterfly garden and the koi pond) and a swimming pool.”
Once native to Britain, beavers were hunted to nationwide extinction by the 1500s thanks to demand for their valuable fur and their scent glands. Now, they’re back and their numbers are thriving, particularly in Kent – there are at least 51 beaver territories along the river Stour, and they can often be spotted in Canterbury.
The US city’s main transport hub, Michigan Central Station, was finally restored to its full glory after the best part of four decades in the void. A performance from singer Diana Ross and  rapper Eminem marked its grand reopening, and our correspondent Chris Leadbeater was in attendance.
A number of airlines unveiled brand-new first-class suites in 2024, including BA and Emirates. However, the new offering from Qantas received rave reviews from aviation expert John Arlidge, who wrote for The Telegraph: “The Australian flag carrier has unveiled the most exclusive, stylish and high-tech airline cabin anywhere outside of a private jet.”
The floating city entered a strange new stage in its history this year, as it started charging day-trippers €5 to step foot in the city. The entry fee was met with a furious backlash, with protesters marching in their thousands holding up banners that read: “Welcome to Veniceland.”
The London railway station was ridiculed for replacing its departure board with a 2,500 sq ft advertising display. One furious passenger took to X, formerly known as Twitter, to ask: “Why is the massive screen just for adverts? I just want to know what platform my train is going from.” Euston has since carried out a U-turn and the screen is now used to display arrivals and departures once again.
Tui was forced to cancel trips to the Finnish town of Kuusamo, near Lapland, after heavy rain washed away all of the snow. This came after a summer of record temperatures. According to the Finnish Meteorological Institute, the average temperature in northern Finland in June, July and August was between 2C and 3.5C higher than usual.
Earlier in the year, Booking.com warned that it had seen a 500 per cent increase in travel-related scams. Why? Experts at the company pointed a finger at the rise of AI, which they say is allowing fraudsters to develop fake adverts and phishing emails in a matter of seconds.
It was a year of frustration and worry at India’s airports. As of November 14, airlines and airports across the country had received a total of 999 hoax bomb threats since the start of the year – 10 times more than the whole of 2023.
The manufacturer has been under the spotlight after a door panel flew off an aircraft, midair, in January 2024. Boeing has faced additional safety and regulatory checks, which has in part contributed to the delayed delivery of new aircraft (such as the 777X and 737 Max) to airlines around the world. Throw in an ongoing staff strike, and 2024 was very much a year to forget for the Seattle-based firm.
The UK flight route with the highest percentage of cancellations (according to Civil Aviation Authority data) was Gatwick to Catania, operated by British Airways. Of the 23 flights scheduled, 14 (60.8 per cent) were cancelled.
The little key-holders have become a symbol of localised frustration against holiday rental firms, such as Airbnb and Vrbo. In Florence, city authorities have banned new short-term rentals in the city centre. In Rome, anti-tourism protesters have taken matters into their own hands by injecting glue into the machines, thus rendering them impossible to unlock.
The Eternal City has been a shadow of its usual self in recent months, with empty fountains and scaffolded monuments. This is because Roberto Gualtieri, the mayor of Rome, commissioned hundreds of infrastructural and maintenance projects ahead of the jubilee year, an event that takes place every quarter of a century and which will see millions of pilgrims visit the city in 2025.
In the year that Wizz unveiled a controversial £414 “all-you-can-fly” scheme, and new routes to Saudi Arabia from next March, it ranked bottom of The Telegraph’s comprehensive study into the world’s best and worst airlines.
Incidents of extreme turbulence are on the rise. One particularly severe case occurred in May, when one man died and 30 passengers were injured during a Singapore Airlines flight. Just four days later, 12 people were hurt on a flight from Doha to Dublin.
The roads in Britain’s oldest national park are increasingly under strain. The Telegraph’s Jack Rear, who visited over the summer, wrote: “Everywhere I drove, vehicles lined the streets, including on grass verges. It made driving around the park fiddly and occasionally dangerous.”
The Icelandic tourist attraction closed to the public on a number of occasions in 2024, due to earthquakes and volcanic activity. Employees described it as a “stressful” time, with sudden evacuations becoming an increasingly common occurrence.
Spare a thought for poor old Drayton House in Northamptonshire, which was forced to employ security guards after flocks of fans of the film Saltburn descended on the Grade I-listed property to take selfies in the location.
Following a period of unrest in the Middle East, there are now only three possible flight routes from Europe to Asia that avoid closed airspace areas. OpsGroup, an outfit for pilots and air traffic controllers, said that the “risk to civil aviation in the region has changed at a pace we have never seen before”.
Throughout the year, there have been a string of protests across Spain, with a particular upswell of activity in the Balearics and the Canary Islands. On a number of occasions, tourists on beaches have found themselves surrounded by placard-wielding protesters complaining about the ill effects of mass tourism.
The Telegraph’s study into the world’s best and worst airports exposed that (with the exception of a few US airports) Britain is unique in charging people to drop off a loved one at the airport terminal.  Of Britain’s 25 biggest airports, 21 charge for picking up or dropping off a passenger at the terminal, even if just for five minutes – and prices are going up.
Private jet passengers will pay a higher rate of air passenger duty (APD) as of 2026, as a result of the Labour Budget. One specific private jet attracted particular attention this year; Just Stop Oil attempted to spray Taylor Swift’s aircraft with orange paint at Stansted Airport, but failed to find it.
The low-cost American airline has long been described as the “Ryanair of the States” – only with even bigger bag fees. Now its future is in peril. On November 18, the budget carrier filed for bankruptcy protection after a run of financial losses and failed merger attempts.
Earlier this year, doctors, lawyers and cabin crew union representatives raised concerns about a social media trend where passengers fasten their seatbelts around their ankles. In a series of TikTok posts, which collectively amassed tens of millions of views, passengers pulled their knees up to their chests with their feet at the edge of their seats, and then fastened the seatbelt around their feet.
Passengers described “carnage” at Birmingham Airport after it took longer than 90 minutes to get through security at the start of the late May bank holiday weekend. There was significant building work at the airport throughout the year, and at times there were delays at security due to confusion around the 100ml liquid rules.
Some Lisbon residents are beginning to grumble that the city centre is going in the same direction as Barcelona, Amsterdam and Venice. One 60-year-old resident, Rosa Santos, told Reuters: “Lisbon has stopped being a city and become an amusement park.” Others have complained about the proliferation of tuk-tuks in the old town.
Mountain rescue workers in Snowdonia warned they were being constantly called out to save walkers as novices attempted to tackle Wales’s highest peaks. On July 21, they had already been called out 97 times up to that point – on more than one occasion, this was due to walkers suffering from panic attacks.
It means a fear of snakes. In January, a Blanford’s bridle snake was discovered on an AirAsia flight from Bangkok to Phuket. In a video widely shared on social media, a member of the cabin crew was seen trying to catch the snake inside an empty water bottle, and it was later pushed into a plastic bag and stowed safely until landing.
The US non-profit organisation Sapien Labs placed the UK second to last in its Mental State of the World report. Using data from 500,000 respondents in 71 countries, it measures how people’s “inner state impacts their ability to function within their life context”. But hey, it could be worse. You could live in Uzbekistan.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.title: Carbon credit schemes ‘uprooting Maasai tribes’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.subtitle: Tanzania’s government has begun evicting people from the Ngorongoro conservation area in a bid to protect wildlife
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/world-news/2.text:
Maasai tribes people are being uprooted to make way for lucrative carbon credit and conservation schemes, activists say.
Tanzania’s government has begun evicting some of the more than 110,000 Maasai from the Ngorongoro conservation area, saying their growing numbers are a threat to the famed savannas and watering holes.
But the tribe’s people and their supporters say the relocation is the latest example of a government elbowing out locals as they try to secure international money from conservation, tourism and climate initiatives.
“The government is doing everything possible to suffocate local communities in order to earn more money from tourism and trophy-hunting,” Moloimet Olemoko, a Maasai herder from Ngorongoro told the Wall Street Journal.
“They are not bothered about the livelihoods of the Maasai.”
Human rights groups have warned that international conservation schemes that attract tourism money, or reward governments for preserving biodiversity or reducing climate change, are being pushed through at the expense of indigenous inhabitants.
Ngorongoro’s wildlife and wilderness are the heart of Tanzania’s tourism industry, which attracts high-paying safaris and hunters. The area is also home to Maasai who were forced to leave the Serengeti in the 1950s after it was made into a national park.
Tanzania’s government says it is now issuing relocation orders to protect wildlife and habitat from overgrazing and overpopulation.
Developing countries such as Tanzania are also increasingly attracted to carbon credit schemes. These allow a polluter to offset the production of carbon dioxide or other climate-heating gases by paying a forest owner to capture those emissions through the carbon absorption power of their trees.
South of Ngorongoro, a local company called Carbon Tanzania is selling carbon credits linked to about 273,000 acres of land that the Maasai and other pastoralist communities have also used for grazing and limited cultivation. The project restricts the cutting down of trees as well as cultivation.
Carbon Tanzania insists it respects indigenous people’s rights and revenue from its projects has improved local education, health and infrastructure.
Nearby, local authorities in February signed a $120,000 deal with a Tanzanian company, Kilombero North Safaris, to run a carbon-credit project in three forests where Maasai communities have grazed their herds, the Journal reported.
A petition from the Greenpeace campaign group alleges the Maasai are being evicted and their ancestral lands sold off for trophy hunting and carbon credits trading “under the guise of conservation”.
In November, lawyers accused neighbouring Kenya of evicting Ogiek hunter-gatherers from their ancestral lands to profit from carbon offsetting schemes.
Two years ago, farmers living in the Republic of the Congo said they had been blocked from accessing their land so that the French oil giant Total Energies and the Congolese government could use it for a carbon offsetting project. Total at the time said it would assess the impact of the scheme.
There have also been accusations of similar evictions in Thailand and Cambodia.
Rob Williams, chair of the Indigenous People’s Law and Policy Programme at the University of Arizona, told the Journal: “These so-called conservation plans are mainly driven by foreign interests, with little regard to the rights of the people.”
Earlier this year, tens of thousands of Maasai blocked the Ngorongoro.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.title: Green energy tycoon ‘gave Labour millions to reduce payout to ex-wife in divorce’
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.subtitle: Dale Vince, who previously bankrolled Just Stop Oil, accused of giving away money in ‘wanton and reckless’ fashion
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.text:
A green energy tycoon who previously bankrolled Just Stop Oil donated millions of pounds to the Labour Party to reduce the amount he would have to pay his ex-wife in a divorce battle, the High Court has been told.
Dale Vince, 63, and his former wife Kate Vince, 50, are in dispute over how money should be split following their divorce, which a judge granted on Tuesday.
Lawyers for Ms Vince claim her ex-husband had been “giving away” their “matrimonial assets”, of which she should be entitled to half, in a “wanton and reckless” fashion.
Barristers for Mr Vince told the court that the increase in donations came from a rise in the value of his businesses, and had “nothing at all to do with” the legal battle.
In written submissions for the hearing, which began on Tuesday, Richard Todd KC, for Ms Vince, said: “It beggars belief that the husband can gift away £14,194,840 of matrimonial assets and say that he should only ever be accountable for such a distribution in the extreme case of a wanton and reckless disposition, albeit this is wanton and reckless.
“The wife’s application was caused entirely by the husband’s refusal to agree to be the custodian of both their money and hold it for them both. She has no difficulty with him spending his half of the money; his demand is that he should be able to spend her half too.
“The post-separation multimillion-pound donations to the Labour Party and to his charitable foundation, and the other charities, should come from his share, it being his unilateral act.”
The court heard that the pair began a relationship in the late 1990s after Ms Vince began working for Mr Vince’s company, Ecotricity.
Mr Vince claimed they separated in 2021, but Ms Vince alleges they were “continuing a physical and emotional relationship right up to February 2022”, the court was told.
Mr Todd said Mr Vince was “penniless” at the start of the relationship and the increase in value of the business “took place within the matrimonial partnership”, meaning that awarding Ms Vince 50 per cent of the pair’s assets “is the fairest outcome”.
The barrister said that between April 2022 and May 2024, Mr Vince had “given £5,460,000 of matrimonial money to the Labour Party”, as well as sums to other organisations.
This included £100,000 to the Cheltenham Muslim Association and £8,464,840 to his foundation, the Green Britain Foundation, which includes support for Forest Green Rovers FC, the National League football side he owns.
It came despite Ms Vince “asking him not to or asking him to confirm that he accepts that these will come out of his own share of the assets”, the court heard.
Lewis Marks KC, for Mr Vince, said in his written submissions that the donations were funded by an “influx of money” stemming from business deals, which “provided the financial wherewithal to make larger donations than previously”.
He added that “an equal division of the overall wealth would be a serious injustice” to Mr Vince, as he made “unmatched endeavour” to the company before and after the relationship.
Mr Marks said: “The impugned donations were made during a period when the value of the business increased hugely, post-separation... The husband’s wish to see a Labour government elected had nothing at all to do with wanting to diminish the wife’s claims, neither does he accept that it will have done so.”
He added: “The wife’s misconception that the funds were ‘theirs’ or ‘hers’, or for that matter ‘his’, is not one which the court should indulge – they were company funds.”
In court, Mr Marks said that Mr Vince “has sought to make this a civilised disengagement”, adding it was a “tragedy that they are here”.
Earlier on Tuesday, Mr Justice Cusworth granted the pair a final divorce, after Ms Vince’s lawyers asked for the decision to be pushed back until after a ruling on the money row.
Mr Todd said in his written submissions that the decision on whether to grant the divorce “is not urgent” and could cause the “potential loss of a share in an honour” given to Mr Vince by the Government in the New Year Honours List because of his donations.
Mr Marks said the issuing of a divorce should not be held up because Ms Vince “wants the possibility of some tag-along title”, which Mr Vince did not believe he would receive.
Mr Justice Cusworth ruled that it would not be “necessary, proportionate and reasonable” to delay issuing a divorce “because there is a possibility that one or the other of the parties at one time in the future might receive some form of honour”.
On Wednesday, the High Court heard Mr Vince does not want to sell “his life’s work” because of his divorce.
The court was told Mr Vince came close to selling his business in 2021-2022 because he thought he might need to for the divorce, and also because he had aspirations of becoming a politician and thought it might pose a conflict of interest.
Mr Vince said: “At the time, Kate and I were just separating – kind of finding our feet in terms of how we were going to move forwards.
“I thought I would probably need to sell the company in order to raise the kind of money I thought she would want.”
Giving another reason, he added: “I had the aspiration to move into politics from where I had been.”
However, the court was told that ultimately the sale did not go ahead for a number of different reasons, including that Mr Vince “reconnected” with business and because he loves what he does.
Taking to the witness box in the London court on Wednesday, Mr Vince said: “I have actually reconnected with the business. I have run this company for 30 years, and we have had many ups and downs.
“It can be really tough but I love what I do.”
Mr Vince also told the court in London that he does not want to “sell his life’s work” because of the divorce.
The hearing is due to conclude later this month.

Dale Vince (left) at a Just Stop Oil protest in London in June 2023
Barristers for Dale Vince told the court the increased donations had ‘nothing at all to do with’ the legal battle

author: Telegraph Reporters

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.title: Miliband’s eco lunacy will wreck Britain and enrich the Chinese dictatorship
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.subtitle: What is the point of achieving net zero here if it means importing Chinese steel made by burning coal?
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.text:
Remember the Ed Stone, that large stone tablet that was met with incredulity and ridicule when it was unveiled by Ed Miliband during Labour’s 2015 election campaign?
Like the bacon sandwich that preceded it, the Ed Stone came to symbolise the ridiculousness of a politician many mistook for Wallace, Gromit’s friend from the animated Aardman films.
It was subsequently thought to have been smashed to pieces with a sledgehammer, very possibly made by Sir Keir Starmer’s father.
But do you know the most preposterous thing about that 8ft 6in tall stone tablet with six election pledges and Miliband’s signature carved into it? There was nothing on the “weird commie slab” (Boris Johnson’s description, not mine) about the environment. Strong economic foundations, a better NHS and more housing? Check. Higher living standards and controls on immigration? Hell, yes! But net zero? Not a dicky bird, despite Miliband having been environment secretary in 2008.
The arbitrary net zero pledge wasn’t actually set in stone until 2019, when the government under Theresa May became the first G7 economy to legislate for it to be met by 2050. Johnson doubled down by committing to decarbonising the UK electricity system by 2035 – with 95 per cent to come from green sources by 2030.
The ambition was already as lofty as an offshore wind turbine, with many questioning how on earth it could be delivered, when Ed Miliband was appointed Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero and quite insanely brought the target forward to 2030. There was absolutely no need for this acceleration beyond a desire to convince lefties tempted to vote for the Greens that Labour could outdo the Tory eco–loons.
As Christmas fast approaches, and we prepare for 2025, it is perhaps worth remembering that there are just 60 months left for the Labour Government to double onshore wind, quadruple offshore wind, and triple solar power. The details of how it might achieve this near impossible goal were set out last week in Miliband’s 138-page Clean Power 2030 Action Plan but, as ever, there is a contradiction at the heart of this Labour “milestone” that has to be addressed – and that’s the increasingly evident human cost.
Miliband, like your average Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil nut, appears to be insisting that the planet must be saved “at all costs” – and despite any sacrifices that may have to be made, personal, economic or otherwise. As he recently insisted: “On climate this transition is unstoppable.” Sorry, unstoppable, even if it causes pensioners to choose between heating and eating?
Before the recent publication of Miliband’s action plan, we had no real idea how he proposed to deliver his maniacal climate goals beyond some guff about creating GB Energy – a company that will not generate any energy at all but instead “invest in a new generation of renewable energy supply”. No one appears to have bothered modelling the impact on consumer bills of a green plan that, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso), needs to raise £40 billion in investment a year, most of it from the private sector. Similarly, it has not been explained how we are to magically develop new carbon capture, storage and green hydrogen technologies within five years, or what contingency plan is in place for when the sun doesn’t shine and the wind doesn’t blow. (Spoiler alert: gas, imported from the US at great cost, because Miliband and Co won’t allow fracking, despite it giving us the “energy security” he craves.)
Labour boasts it will “save £93 billion for UK households”, yet Miliband has already had to back away from his pledge that £300 a year will be shaved off the average energy bill. The sums don’t quite add up, since the UK is currently paying more for energy than most of the rest of Europe – despite deriving 25 per cent more energy from wind, and 3.9 per cent more from solar than a decade ago.
Back then, people had a say over what was built in their back yard, but we now know Miliband’s eco-quest is contingent on riding roughshod over the rights of communities to object to new pylons or wind farms in their neighbourhoods. Nearly 1,000km (620 miles) of new power lines will be required to connect new renewable energy to the grid. Meanwhile, the liberalisation of planning laws will make it easier to progress onshore farms larger than 100MW, which in some cases require hundreds of acres of land (no doubt surrendered by farmers priced out by the inheritance tax hike).
But despite Labour’s decades-long commitment to devolution, anyone wanting to raise a local objection is now to be viewed as a “blocker, delayer and obstructionist”, according to Miliband. So much for the Prime Minister’s declaration that he wants to “empower communities”.
Similarly, Labour is all for job creation, provided it isn’t in the North Sea, where the future of 30,000 workers is hanging in the balance thanks to Labour’s plan to halt new oil and gas exploration. The GMB union has rightly questioned Chancellor Rachel Reeves’s completely uncorroborated promise of creating 650,000 “green” jobs.
Gary Smith, the GMB union leader, has already called for the Government to stop “decarbonisation through deindustrialisation”. Referring to the loss of 2,500 jobs at Port Talbot steelworks, he asked: “Thousands of jobs are going to go, a community is going to be hollowed out. We’re going to see huge reductions in our carbon emissions, but at what price?”
We are now importing ever greater amounts of steel from China, which burns huge amounts of coal to produce it. It defies common sense.
Speaking of China, Miliband’s plot to build one billion solar panels across Britain by 2035 is an absolute gift to President Xi Jinping, whose despotic regime made 97 per cent of the solar panels installed across Europe in 2023.Chinese solar panels are cheaper because they’re made with the help of nearly three million Uyghur and Kazakh people from Xinjiang in forced labour camps.
The US and EU have both passed laws banning solar products made by slave labour, but not the UK. Instead, Miliband decided to approve three huge solar farms in July, despite repeated warnings about alleged human rights abuses.
China also has a near monopoly on the rare earths used to make the permanent magnets in wind turbines and electric vehicles as well as a large market share in the production of battery anodes, high-quality spherical graphite, and the processing of manganese, which presumably explains why Miliband is heading to China in the new year as the Government continues to “renew relations”. Progressive stuff.
We are lining the pockets of the world’s largest emitter of CO2, to reduce our 1 per cent to zero per cent. It’s as ludicrous and laughable as Ed and his stone.

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.title: Greta Thunberg’s descent from climate darling to militant pro-Palestine mouthpiece
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.subtitle: Once lauded as an environmental star, Greta Thunberg appears to have embraced thuggish tactics over delicate diplomacy
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.text:
In 2019 Time magazine named Greta Thunberg its youngest-ever Person of the Year, as world leaders and commentators all hastened to bask in the reflected glory of this new environmental star. Thunberg’s powerful influence was even dubbed the “Greta effect” thanks to thousands of students remaking themselves in her climate warrior image. But, five years on, that blind hero worship of an increasingly militant Thunberg looks naïve at best and dangerous at worst.
Speaking at a rally in the German city of Mannheim on Friday, Thunberg, 21, was a far cry from that angelic Time cover, which followed a keynote speech delivered to the UN in September 2019. “F--- Germany,” she said into the microphone on Friday, before descending into giggles as the 700-strong crowd of protesters whooped and clapped. Thunberg added: “And f--- Israel.”
The event was billed as a Palestine and climate movement solidarity rally, but the profanity-spewing Swede seemed most intent on stoking anger towards other nations. Thunberg was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize five times between 2019 and 2023. She probably shouldn’t hold out hope for a sixth nod.
It puts figures such as Barack Obama, Ed Miliband, now the Energy Secretary, and António Guterres, the UN Secretary General, in an embarrassing position after fervently backing Thunberg – even if that meant overlooking some of her more uncompromising views and tactics. Others feel vindicated in having voiced opposition.
“Not so long ago, anyone breathing a word of criticism against St Greta was immediately labelled a misogynistic bully and a climate change denier,” recalls Toby Young, director of the Free Speech Union. “I myself was on the receiving end of a mobbing on social media for questioning her expertise in climate science, given that she left school at the age of 14. Now, it looks very much as if the heretics were right and the worshippers were credulous fools.”
One former cabinet minister says: “There’s been a whole lot of groupthink around the issue of climate change where everyone competed to wear the biggest hair shirt and shut down the most industries in order to placate people who worshipped Greta Thunberg. But those policies are having a major impact on the economy. If I had the choice of listening to Greta Thunberg or to someone facing redundancy, I know who I’d listen to.”
A media advisor who has worked with Labour says: “It illustrates the danger of using a wild card like Greta – she might fit some of your messaging, or reach different audiences, but you have no control. Now she’s showing her full contempt for democracy and the rule of law. She’s left a lot of people with egg on their faces.”
Thunberg’s remarks at the Mannheim rally drew blistering criticism. German politician Manuel Hagel told the Jerusalem Post that Thunberg was “moving very consciously in close proximity to anti-Semitism”, while American campaign group StopAntisemitism labelled Thunberg a “climate activist turned Hamas shill”. They added: “Someone should remind Greta that Israel is a global leader in solving the climate challenge.”
But it seems that Thunberg is no longer interested in such nuance, nor in the delicate work of global diplomacy. Instead she has embraced thuggish, even criminal, tactics.
In June 2023 she was charged with disobeying a police order in Malmö, Sweden, while taking part in a traffic-disrupting Reclaim the Future protest. She was sentenced to pay fines of 2,500 Krona (£179), but just hours after that conviction, Thunberg, undeterred, attended another protest which again blocked oil trucks. That October she was found guilty of disobeying a police order to disperse and fined, although she avoided a potential prison sentence of up to six months.
Yet Thunberg remained committed to that extreme course of action. She was arrested in London in October 2023 and charged with failure to comply with a lawful order to disperse, and has joined forces with the controversial Extinction Rebellion for rallies in which they blocked traffic near The Hague in the Netherlands and in Helsinki. At the Hague rally in July, police had to deploy water cannons when protestors, including Thunberg, refused to disperse.
However, it’s not just her methods which are proving divisive, but her entwining of those long-held climate views with pro-Palestinian activism. In October 2023 Thunberg urged her social media followers to support Palestinians in Gaza, but made no mention of Hamas’s October 7 attack. She added another post the following day with a belated condemnation of October 7, though with a call for “an immediate ceasefire”, amid Israel’s initial military response to the attack. Palestine has since featured in many of her speeches.
In May 2024 Thunberg joined thousands of angry protestors at a Stop Israel rally outside the venue for the Eurovision Song Contest in Malmö. The 20-year-old singer Eden Golan, who was representing Israel in the competition, and who had separately received death threats, was ordered to stay in her hotel room for her own security. But Thunberg proudly told Reuters, of the protest: “Young people are leading the way and showing the world how we should react to this.”
Unsurprisingly, other climate activists are now distancing themselves from Thunberg – including the German chapter of Fridays for Future, the international movement of students who skip school on Fridays to hold climate demonstrations. In November 2023 chapter head Luisa Neubauer criticised Thunberg’s “one-sided” view of the war in Gaza, and told Die Zeit that the German branch would have to examine “with whom we still have a basis to work based on common values”.
But what about the many other figures who eagerly aligned themselves with Thunberg? They range from leading politicians to Hollywood A-listers and even Pope Francis. In April 2019 the latter gave her his blessing to continue her work.
Former American President Barack Obama was equally enamoured when he met Thunberg in September that year. Afterwards he wrote on social media that she was “one of our planet’s greatest advocates”, “unafraid to push for real action”, and that she embodied his and Michelle’s vision for their Obama Foundation: “A future shaped by young leaders like [Thunberg].”
What must Obama have been thinking when he read Thunberg’s tirade on X last month ahead of the US election, in which she raged that no matter which candidate won, America would still be “an imperialist, hyper-capitalist world power that will ultimately continue to lead the world further into a racist, unequal world with an ever increasingly escalating climate and environmental emergency.” Thunberg urged American citizens to “fill the streets, block, organise, boycott, occupy”.
It’s extraordinary to think that back in February 2019 Thunberg was standing on a stage with then-President of the European Commission Jean-Claude Juncker as he made climate commitments for the next EU budget, after praising her for bringing about change. Thunberg was also fêted in April that year by British politicians.
Michael Gove said that Thunberg’s was “the voice of our conscience”, while Ed Miliband gushed: “You have woken us up. We thank you”, and Jeremy Corbyn wrote on social media that it was “a pleasure welcoming UK youth climate strikers and Greta Thunberg to Parliament”. Guterres met Thunberg in June 2019, when he declared: “I trust young people like Greta Thunberg to push my generation, to push their parents, to push societies to save our planet & our future.” Later that year, he invited the then 16-year-old to address the UN’s Climate Action Summit in New York.
Meanwhile Leonard DiCaprio shared pictures of himself with Thunberg on Instagram in November 2019, calling her “a leader of our time” – shortly after she addressed the Cop25 summit in Madrid. The BBC also got in on the action, inviting her to guest edit Radio Four’s Today programme in December. Thunberg’s edition featured interviews with David Attenborough and Bank of England chief Mark Carney.
Thunberg has essentially thrown that idolisation back in everyone’s faces. In 2021 she mocked Boris Johnson and others in her opening speech for a youth climate summit in Italy, claiming that “our so-called leaders” offered words but no action.
Instead of supporting open debate and free speech, in December 2022 she backed Edinburgh University students who blocked the screening of a film, Adult Human Female, that the union branded “transphobic”.
Allying yourself with Thunberg was once a cheap and easy win. Now, it costs the earth.

Thunberg was removed by police at a Stop Israel rally outside the venue for the Eurovision Song Contest in Malmö in May

https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.title: Grantchester in uproar over parish magazine praise for jailed Just Stop Oil protester
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.subtitle: Residents of leafy Cambridgeshire village where TV detective show is set rail at supportive profile of eco-activist who caused mayhem on M25
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2024/12.text:
A row has erupted in Grantchester after its parish magazine printed a supportive profile of a jailed eco-activist
Residents of the leafy Cambridgeshire village, where the ITV detective drama is set in the 1950s, are up in arms over the article about Louise Lancaster, a Just Stop Oil protester.
The 58-year-old teacher was jailed with four others in July after being found guilty of conspiring to block traffic on the M25 in November 2022.
But she has been lauded as a “friend and neighbour”, a “trusted member of the village” and “one of us” in the article published in December’s edition of the monthly Grantchester Parish Magazine.
The profile, written by villager Debbie Meller, tells of her comfortable life inside prison tending vegetables, doing yoga exercises and taking part in Parkrun jogs.
The article caused an uproar in the village and prompted calls for a boycott of the magazine.
“This has caused a divide in the village,” one local told MailOnline. “Grantchester is tiny, and it’s made up of some really big houses and the rest of us.
“It feels like most of Lancaster’s support live in these big houses, and it’s the rest of us that had to put up with the disruption at the time.”
Villagers also took to a local Facebook group to complain about the article, but Lancaster’s supporters hit back as they insisted: “Everyone’s entitled to their opinion but this is about peaceful protesters being jailed.”
Notable residents of the village include Jeffrey Archer, the novelist and former politician.
David Gilmour, the Pink Floyd guitarist, grew up in the village and Rupert Brooke, the early 20th-century poet, stayed at the village’s Old Vicarage before the First World War.
TV’s Grantchester portrays the crime-solving escapades of Det Ch Insp Geordie Keating (Robson Green) and a succession of Anglican vicars.
The article claimed that Lancaster found it “rather frustrating” to be initially sent to HMP Bronzefield, a category A women’s prison near Ashford, Surrey, which the article describes as “where the UK’s most notorious criminals are held including, most recently, Lucy Letby”.
“At Bronzefield, all the inmates had to use their one hour outside their cell to wash, buy provisions, stay in contact with family and take exercise, so she found it rather frustrating,” it reads.
But following the intervention of Pippa Heylings, the Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire, she was moved to HMP Send, near Woking, Surrey, where “her circumstances are much improved”.
“Unlike Bronzefield, she has a room to herself so isn’t forced to watch TV from morning until night,” the article reads.
At Send, Lancaster is said to jog around the grounds on the prison Parkrun, grow vegetables in its gardens for £1.50 a shift and do yoga exercises in her cell using a mat sent to her by friends.
She is also said to enjoy birdwatching from her window, swapping books with fellow inmates and enjoying a “lime spritzer” – sparkling water and lime juice – as a treat every Friday.
“Despite being locked in her cell from 6pm (5pm at weekends), she is finding pleasure in the small things,” the profile reads.
Lancaster is said to receive phone calls, emails and letters from the outside world, and she sticks postcards and photographs onto the walls of her cell using toothpaste.
The article goes on to describe her desire to be moved to an open prison during the “challenging chapter of her life”.
In July, Lancaster was jailed for four years alongside Extinction Rebellion co-founder Roger Hallam, 58, Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 34, and Cressida Gethin, 22, after being convicted of conspiracy to intentionally cause a public nuisance.
Southwark Crown Court had heard that each of the defendants had recruited activists over a Zoom call to take part in the motorway demonstration, which the prosecution said had caused economic damage of nearly £750,000 and cost the police £1 million.
The disruption allegedly caused more than 50,000 hours of traffic delays, affecting the journeys of more than 700,000 vehicles.
Grantchester Parish Magazine was approached for comment.
A source close to the magazine said the original complainant was not thought to be a resident of the village.
author: Tim Sigsworth
